claims.claim: The TGF-β superfamily member protein GDF11 decreases with age and restoring its levels alone is sufficient to reverse age-related dysfunction in the skeletal system.
claims.source: Follow-up studies show the TGF-β superfamily member protein GDF11 decreases with age and restoring its levels-alone is sufficient to reverse age-related dysfunction in the skeletal system (Sinha et al., 2014) as well as restoration of the neurogenic niche (Katsimpardi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Sinha et al., 2014 and Katsimpardi et al., 2014

claims.claim: Restoring GDF11 levels is sufficient to restore the neurogenic niche.
claims.source: Follow-up studies show the TGF-β superfamily member protein GDF11 decreases with age and restoring its levels-alone is sufficient to reverse age-related dysfunction in the skeletal system (Sinha et al., 2014) as well as restoration of the neurogenic niche (Katsimpardi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Katsimpardi et al., 2014

claims.claim: An initial study found that young plasma is not able to extend lifespan in aged mice.
claims.source: Despite the observed benefits of young serum in older mice, an initial study found that young plasma is not able to extend lifespan in aged mice (Shytikov et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Shytikov et al., 2014

claims.claim: Globally knocking out the capsaicin receptor TRPV1 in mice causes no change in body weight or circulating GH/IGF-1, but increases metabolic activity and energy expenditure and increases lifespan by 10–20%.
claims.source: To that end, globally knocking out the capsaicin receptor TRPV1 in mice causes no change in body weight or circulating growth hormone (GH)/IGF-1, but increases metabolic activity and energy expenditure and increases lifespan by 10–20% (Riera et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Riera et al., 2014

claims.claim: In worms, knocking out the TRPV-1 orthologues, osm-9 and ocr-2, requires the transcription factor CRTC-1 to influence lifespan.
claims.source: In worms, knocking out the TRPV-1 orthologues, osm-9 and ocr-2, requires the transcription factor CRTC-1 to influence lifespan.
claims.evidence: Supported by the preceding citation to Riera et al., 2014

claims.claim: In mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) primary neuron cultures, TRPV-1 is necessary for nuclear translocation of CRTC-1.
claims.source: In mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) primary neuron cultures, TRPV-1 is also necessary for nuclear translocation of CRTC-1.
claims.evidence: Supported by the preceding citation to Riera et al., 2014

claims.claim: CRTC-1 interacts with CREB in DRG neurons to regulate secretion of the neuropeptides calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P at pancreatic beta cells.
claims.source: CRTC-1 interacts with CREB in DRG neurons to regulate secretion of the neuropeptides calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P at pancreatic beta cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by the preceding citation to Riera et al., 2014

claims.claim: TRPV-1 knockout mice have reduced CRTC-1 activity which reduces CGRP expression and increases pancreatic insulin secretion leading to better glucose tolerance and longevity.
claims.source: The model suggests TRPV-1 knockout mice have reduced CRTC-1 activity which reduces CGRP expression and increases pancreatic insulin secretion leading to better glucose tolerance and longevity.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the cited study

claims.claim: Recent data from invertebrates supports the idea of non-canonical cell non-autonomous mechanisms where the peripheral tissues use a retrograde signal back to the nervous system to maintain or further modify physiology.
claims.source: However, recent data from invertebrates supports the idea of non-canonical cell non-autonomous mechanisms where the peripheral tissues use a retrograde signal back to the nervous system to maintain or further modify physiology (Minniti et al., 2019; Bouagnon et al., 2019; Demontis and Perrimon, 2010; Ulgherait et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Minniti et al., 2019; Bouagnon et al., 2019; Demontis and Perrimon, 2010; Ulgherait et al., 2014

claims.claim: Just a day of hypoxia can extend lifespan in a worm.
claims.source: Studies show that just a day of hypoxia (Mehta et al., 2009), for example, can extend lifespan in a worm, but whether that is just due to the persistent benefits of physiological changes made during that day or due to lasting epigenetic changes in peripheral tissues is an open question.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mehta et al., 2009

claims.claim: Serotonin antagonism can extend adult neuroplasticity and lifespan.
claims.source: More specifically, it is intriguing that serotonin antagonism can extend adult neuroplasticity and lifespan (Petrascheck et al., 2009; Bazopoulou et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Petrascheck et al., 2009; Bazopoulou et al., 2017

claims.claim: Two drug combinations synergistically improve lifespan and healthspan in C. elegans, requiring TGF-β signaling and increased levels of monounsaturated fatty acids.
claims.source: For example, Admasu et. al identified two drug combinations that synergistically improve lifespan and healthspan. The synergistic effects of both drug combinations required TGF-β signaling and increased levels of monounsaturated fatty acids (Admasu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Admasu et al., 2018

claims.claim: Simultaneous inhibition of mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase, mTOR complex 1, and glycogen synthase kinase-3 acted additively to increase Drosophila lifespan by 48%.
claims.source: Simultaneous inhibition of mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase, mTOR complex 1, and glycogen synthase kinase-3 acted additively to increase Drosophila lifespan by 48% (Castillo-Quan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Castillo-Quan et al., 2019

results.result: By 2050, the number of US citizens over the age of 65 will reach nearly 100 million, more than twice as many as today.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is supported by a citation to United Nations, 2015. This is a demographic projection from an authoritative source and provides appropriate context for the manuscript's focus on aging research.

results.result: Organismal lifespan is a genetically modifiable trait, as demonstrated by mutations in the C. elegans insulin-like growth factor receptor daf-2 that can double lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C9 are well-supported by foundational citations (Friedman and Johnson, 1988; Kenyon et al., 1993; Kimura, 1997). These are landmark studies in the aging field that established the genetic basis of lifespan regulation.

results.result: Environmental factors such as food perception or oxygen levels can modify longevity in model organisms.
results.evaluation: Claim C3 is supported by multiple citations (Libert et al., 2007; Kaeberlein et al., 2006; Mehta et al., 2009) demonstrating that environmental interventions can modulate lifespan, complementing genetic approaches.

results.result: The concept of cell signaling through receptor proteins was established by John Langley and validated through discoveries including Rita Levi-Montalcini's identification of nerve growth factor.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C5 provide historical context for cell signaling, supported by appropriate citations (Maehle, 2004; Cohen, 1965; Paton and Rang, 1965) and established scientific knowledge.

results.result: Many signaling pathways that improve longevity act through cell non-autonomous mechanisms, originating in sensory cells that signal to peripheral tissues, and activation of these stress response pathways is often sufficient to improve health and longevity even without stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 are supported by multiple high-profile citations (Schinzel and Dillin, 2015; Leiser et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2013; Riera et al., 2014; Ro et al., 2016) establishing the central thesis of the review.

results.result: Mosaic expression studies identified cell lineages requiring daf-2 mutations for lifespan extension, representing the first clear demonstration of cell non-autonomous activity in aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C11 and C12 are supported by citation to Apfeld and Kenyon, 1998, a foundational study in the field. The historical significance claim (C12) is a reasonable inference from the context.

results.result: daf-2 mutants require daf-16/FOXO for lifespan extension, with most effects occurring through cell-autonomous intestinal transcription, though some target genes influence muscle aging cell non-autonomously and intestinal daf-16 expression induces target genes in other tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 are supported by appropriate citations (Gottlieb and Ruvkun, 1994; Libina et al., 2003; McCormick et al., 2012) demonstrating both cell-autonomous and non-autonomous functions of daf-16.

results.result: Tissue-specific rescue experiments show that neuronal daf-2/age-1 expression blocks lifespan extension while muscle expression restores metabolic function, demonstrating that metabolism and aging are separable yet interrelated with bi-directional signaling between tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C20 are supported by citation to Wolkow et al., 2000. The inference about separability and bi-directional signaling (C19-C20) is reasonable based on the experimental evidence.

results.result: Ablation of amphid neuron ciliated projections extends lifespan in a daf-16-dependent manner, with daf-16 target genes expressed in mechanosensory neurons including fkh-9/FOXL1 which is required for daf-2 lifespan extension.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by citations to Apfeld and Kenyon, 1999; Alcedo and Kenyon, 2004; and Kaletsky et al., 2016, demonstrating the role of sensory neurons in longevity regulation.

results.result: The insulin-like peptide ins-7 is required for daf-2 RNAi-mediated lifespan extension, and C. elegans has approximately 40 insulin-like peptides that can modulate lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C24 and C25 are supported by citations to Silva et al., 2013 and De Rosa et al., 2019, highlighting the complexity of insulin-like signaling in C. elegans.

results.result: Germline signaling regulates insulin signaling by decreasing daf-16 activity, and germline ablation activates a daf-12-dependent sterol signaling pathway that produces lipophilic signals affecting other tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 are supported by citations to Hsin and Kenyon, 1999; Yamawaki et al., 2010; and McCormick et al., 2012, demonstrating germline-to-soma signaling in longevity.

results.result: The microRNA mir-71 is necessary for germline mutant longevity and its overexpression extends lifespan beyond germline mutations alone, with neuronal mir-71 sufficient for rescue and requiring intestinal daf-16.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are all supported by citation to Boulias and Horvitz, 2012, demonstrating a role for microRNAs in cell non-autonomous longevity regulation.

results.result: Absence of gonadal stem cell signaling activates intestinal skn-1/Nrf2 and increases circulating fatty acids, which may induce skn-1 nuclear localization to enhance lipid metabolism and increase lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C35 are supported by citation to Steinbaugh et al., 2015, but C36 is speculative. The mechanistic link between circulating lipids and skn-1 activation requires further validation.

results.result: The nuclear hormone receptor nhr-49/HNF4α regulates glp-1-mediated longevity and lipid metabolism, with overexpression extending lifespan in a daf-16- and glp-1-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C37 and C38 are supported by citation to Ratnappan et al., 2014, linking nuclear hormone receptor signaling to germline-mediated longevity.

results.result: The AMPK ortholog aak-2 promotes longevity when overexpressed by suppressing CREB/CRTC-1 transcriptional regulation, and neuron-specific crtc-1 knockout extends lifespan without pleiotropic effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by citations to Apfeld et al., 2004; Mair et al., 2011; and Burkewitz et al., 2015, demonstrating AMPK's role in cell non-autonomous longevity regulation.

results.result: nhr-49/HNF4α is activated by AAK-2 and its neuronal expression is required for AAK-2-mediated lifespan extension, with neuronal CRTC-1 modifying intestinal AAK-2 activity through octopamine signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by citations to Moreno-Arriola et al., 2016 and related studies, though C45 involves some inference about the signaling mechanism.

results.result: Octopamine is synthesized in RIC head neurons and its receptors are expressed in inner neurons but not peripheral tissues, suggesting it acts as an initiating signal rather than a direct signal to downstream tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by citations to Alkema et al., 2005; Suo et al., 2006; and Mills et al., 2012. The inference in C48 is reasonable based on the expression patterns.

results.result: GABAergic signaling and neuron excitability inversely change throughout the life of short- and long-lived animals.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2018, providing evidence for age-related changes in neuronal signaling.

results.result: Downregulation of TORC1 components like raga-1 increases lifespan but requires neuronal aak-2 activity, with neuronal TORC1 expression sufficient to shorten lifespan and neuronal raga-1 activity leading to mitochondrial fragmentation in peripheral tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by citations to Schreiber et al., 2010 and Zhang et al., 2019, demonstrating neuronal control of peripheral metabolism through TORC1 signaling.

results.result: Acute moderate stress can trigger hormetic effects that extend lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by citation to Calabrese et al., 2015, establishing the hormesis concept relevant to the subsequent discussion of stress responses.

results.result: Neuronal knockdown of the electron transport chain component cco-1 increases lifespan without pleiotropic phenotypes by altering mitochondrial homeostasis in peripheral tissues through the mt-UPR but not daf-16.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by citation to Durieux et al., 2011, demonstrating cell non-autonomous mitochondrial stress signaling.

results.result: vps-35 mutants lack peripheral mt-UPR, and VPS-35 is involved in recycling Wnt signaling components, with the Wnt receptor egl-20 necessary and sufficient for cell non-autonomous mt-UPR induction and longevity.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2018a and Prasad and Clark, 2006, identifying Wnt signaling as a mediator of mt-UPR cell non-autonomous effects.

results.result: Neuronal serotonin production is necessary for cell non-autonomous mt-UPR even though loss of individual known serotonin receptors has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C63 are supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018a, but the paradox of requiring serotonin without identified receptors suggests incomplete mechanistic understanding or redundancy.

results.result: Neuronal activation of the ER-UPR through xbp-1s is sufficient to enhance stress resistance and extend lifespan, with expression in nervous system or intestine extending lifespan and neuronal expression sufficient for stress resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 are supported by multiple citations (Taylor and Dillin, 2013; Imanikia et al., 2019b; Frakes et al., 2020; Daniele et al., 2020; Imanikia et al., 2019a), establishing ER-UPR as a key cell non-autonomous longevity pathway.

results.result: Neuronal ER-UPR releases a signal conferring xbp-1s upregulation in intestines that rescues motility in proteotoxicity models.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by citation to Imanikia et al., 2019b, demonstrating functional consequences of ER-UPR cell non-autonomous signaling.

results.result: Glial expression of xbp-1s extends lifespan and activates ER-UPR in peripheral tissues through neuropeptide signaling, though the specific neuropeptide remains unidentified among hundreds of candidates.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by citations to Frakes et al., 2020 and Li et al., 1999a/b. The identification of glia as a source and neuropeptides as mediators is significant, though the specific signal remains unknown.

results.result: xbp-1 activity, not pek-1 or atf-6, is key to modifying lifespan through ER-UPR.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is supported by citation to Frakes et al., 2020, identifying the specific ER-UPR branch responsible for longevity effects.

results.result: Neuronal xbp-1s activation results in changes in fat metabolism and oleic acid accumulation, possibly through increased lysosomal gene expression enhancing protease activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by citation to Imanikia et al., 2019a, but C74 is speculative about the mechanism. The connection between xbp-1s and lysosomal function requires further validation.

results.result: The lifespan phenotype of xbp-1s animals requires lipid depletion, and enhanced intestinal lipid depletion through ehbp-1 overexpression modestly extends lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C75 and C76 are supported by citation to Daniele et al., 2020, linking ER-UPR effects to lipid metabolism.

results.result: Longevity varies inversely with temperature in C. elegans, but many pro-longevity mutations have temperature-specific effects, suggesting genes actively influence lifespan at various temperatures beyond simple thermodynamic effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are supported by citation to Miller et al., 2017 and established knowledge. The genetic modulation of temperature-dependent lifespan is well-documented.

results.result: Post-reproductive adulthood in C. elegans is accompanied by an abrupt decline in protein quality control, and maintaining heat stress response ability is a hallmark of long-lived animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C80 and C81 are supported by citations to Walther et al., 2015; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015; and Santra et al., 2019, establishing the importance of proteostasis in aging.

results.result: Key signaling components of amphid neurons (gcy-3 and ttx-3) are necessary for proper heat shock response induction, implicating an unknown neurotransmitter in this signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C82 and C83 are supported by citation to Prahlad et al., 2008, though the specific neurotransmitter remains unidentified.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of AFD thermosensory neurons triggers serotonin release from ADF neurons that activates HSF-1 through the ser-1 receptor, though no direct connection exists between AFD and ADF neurons suggesting intermediate signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by citation to Tatum et al., 2015 and knowledge of C. elegans connectivity. The lack of direct connection (C87) is an important observation suggesting circuit complexity.

results.result: Neuronal hsf-1 overexpression is sufficient to increase stress resistance and longevity, requiring intact AFD/AIY signaling possibly through pat-4/ILK, with intestinal daf-16 required for lifespan but not stress resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 are supported by citations to Lee and Kenyon, 2009; Douglas et al., 2015; Prahlad et al., 2008; and Kumsta et al., 2014, demonstrating the separation of stress resistance and longevity pathways.

results.result: AFD neurons and ASJ sensory neurons respond to warm temperatures through tax-2/tax-4 channels, deploying daf-9 to inhibit daf-12 for lifespan extension at 25°C, distinct from heat shock response as heat shock proteins are not upregulated at this temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 are supported by citations to Lee and Kenyon, 2009; Zhang et al., 2018a; and Artan et al., 2016, distinguishing warm temperature sensing from heat shock response.

results.result: TRPA-1 detects cold temperatures in chemosensory neurons and signals through PKC-2 to increase intestinal DAF-16 activity and lifespan at cooler temperatures, with human TRPA-1 showing functional conservation.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by citation to Xiao et al., 2013, demonstrating cold-sensing mechanisms and suggesting evolutionary conservation.

results.result: trpa-1 expression in IL1 neurons is necessary and sufficient for cold-sensing lifespan modulation, requiring glutamate secretion to an intermediate neuron (as MGL-1 is neuron-specific), then serotonin signaling from NSM neurons to intestinal ser-7 receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 are supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018b, providing one of the most complete circuit descriptions in the manuscript.

results.result: Dietary restriction is a conserved longevity intervention, and the first report of DR acting through sensory cell non-autonomous signaling identified SKN-1 in ASI sensory neurons as leading to increased respiration and lifespan, establishing food perception as a major driver of DR benefits.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by citations to McCay et al., 1935; Fontana and Partridge, 2015; and Bishop and Guarente, 2007, establishing the foundational role of sensory perception in DR.

results.result: ASI and ASJ sensory neurons shorten lifespan through ins-6 expression during food perception, with ins-6 released upon feeding and overexpression blocking longevity effects of fasting, suggesting an unknown inverse signal during fasting.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by citation to Artan et al., 2016, though C112 is speculative about the inverse signal mechanism.

results.result: In the absence of food, nematodes increase movement and stop pharyngeal pumping, and upon perceiving attractive odorants, serotonin triggers intestinal acox-1-mediated fat catabolism that is necessary and sufficient for behavioral changes, with egl-2 likely signaling satiety back to serotonin neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C118 are supported by citations to You et al., 2008; McCloskey et al., 2017; Waggoner et al., 1998; Srinivasan et al., 2008; and Zheng et al., 2018, demonstrating bidirectional signaling between neurons and intestine.

results.result: Antagonizing serotonin signaling through mianserin extends lifespan and is non-additive with dietary restriction.
results.evaluation: Claim C119 is supported by citation to Petrascheck et al., 2009, suggesting serotonin antagonism and DR act through overlapping pathways.

results.result: Recognition of low-oxygen conditions or HIF-1 stabilization extends nematode longevity through FMO-2, with neuronal HIF-1 stabilization sufficient to induce intestinal fmo-2 via serotonergic signaling, and intestinal FMO-2 overexpression sufficient for lifespan extension.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C124 are supported by citations to Mehta et al., 2009; Leiser et al., 2013; and Leiser et al., 2015, identifying FMO-2 as a key mediator of hypoxic longevity.

results.result: FMO induction has been found in multiple mammalian longevity models including dietary restriction, suggesting a conserved role in promoting long-term health.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 is supported by citations to Swindell, 2009 and Steinbaugh et al., 2012, suggesting translational potential of FMO findings.

results.result: Reduced insulin signaling increases fly lifespan, with mutations in dInR or chico exerting non-autonomous effects on aging and extending lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C126 and C127 are supported by citations to Kannan and Fridell, 2013; Clancy et al., 2001; and Tatar et al., 2001, establishing conservation of insulin signaling effects in Drosophila.

results.result: Overexpression of dFOXO or dPTEN in fat body extends fly lifespan, indicating that insulin signaling acts cell non-autonomously to control aging with bi-directional signaling between peripheral tissues and neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 are supported by citations to Giannakou et al., 2004 and Hwangbo et al., 2004, with C130 being a reasonable inference from the tissue-specific effects.

results.result: Drosophila insulin-like peptides (dilps) are produced in insulin producing cells (IPCs) in the brain and released into hemolymph to signal through a single insulin receptor, with dilp2, dilp3, dilp5, and dilp6 being the most studied in aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 are supported by citations to Brogiolo et al., 2001; Colombani et al., 2012; Grönke et al., 2010; Bai et al., 2012; and Broughton et al., 2010, establishing the Drosophila insulin signaling system.

results.result: Partial ablation of IPCs reduces insulin signaling and increases lifespan, knocking down GABA-B receptors in IPCs decreases DILP secretion and lifespan under starvation, and mutation of dilp2, dilp3, and dilp5 together or dilp2 alone increases lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C136 are supported by citations to Broughton et al., 2005; Haselton et al., 2010; Enell et al., 2010; and Grönke et al., 2010, demonstrating the role of specific dilps in longevity.

results.result: Induction of dilp6 in fat body tissue promotes longevity, though it is unclear whether this is a direct effect or due to decreased DILP2 secretion from IPCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C137 and C138 are supported by citation to Bai et al., 2012, acknowledging mechanistic uncertainty.

results.result: Extended lifespan from increased dFOXO expression in pericerebral fat body may result from decreased dilp2 expression in IPCs.
results.evaluation: Claim C139 is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2005, suggesting a mechanism for fat body-to-brain signaling.

results.result: dilp1 plays a role in promoting lifespan potentially through induction of adipokinetic hormone (AKH), a functional homolog of mammalian glucagon that increases fly lifespan and fat metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C140 and C141 are supported by citations to Post et al., 2019; Bednarova et al., 2013; Waterson et al., 2014; and Waterson et al., 2015, identifying AKH as a potential mediator.

results.result: The link between neuronal dilp manipulation and peripheral FOXO is less clear in Drosophila than C. elegans, with loss of dilp2 not influencing known FOXO target gene expression, suggesting FOXO-independent pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C142 and C143 are supported by citation to Post et al., 2019, highlighting important differences between organisms.

results.result: Flies lacking IPCs or dilps 2, 3, and 5 exhibit abnormal responses to diet manipulation, though dFOXO mutation leaves the response largely intact, and loss of dFOXO only partially rescues chico mutant longevity.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C146 are supported by citations to Grönke et al., 2010; Broughton et al., 2010; Giannakou et al., 2008; and Yamamoto and Tatar, 2011, further supporting FOXO-independent mechanisms.

results.result: Neuronal or intestinal activation of AMPK or Atg1 induces autophagy in both brain and gut to slow aging, with dilps mediating inter-tissue responses and AMPK activation causing whole-body metabolic remodeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C149 are supported by citation to Ulgherait et al., 2014, demonstrating bidirectional AMPK signaling effects.

results.result: Global knockdown of ETC components in complexes I, III, IV, and V extends fly lifespan without inhibiting complex formation or ATP production, and neuronal knockdown of complexes I and IV is sufficient for lifespan extension.
results.evaluation: Claims C150 and C151 are supported by citation to Copeland et al., 2009, demonstrating cell non-autonomous effects of mitochondrial dysfunction.

results.result: Muscle-specific knockdown of ETC complex I increases ROS and activates mito-UPR and ImpL2, with mito-UPR preserving muscle function and ImpL2 signaling to brain and fat body to decrease insulin signaling, both likely contributing to longevity.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C154 are supported by citation to Owusu-Ansah et al., 2013, identifying dual pathways for mitochondrial stress signaling.

results.result: Knockdown of ETC ND75 in complex I results in smaller flies, similar to the nematode ortholog isp-1 mutants, suggesting pathway conservation.
results.evaluation: Claim C155 is supported by citation to Feng et al., 2001, providing evidence for evolutionary conservation.

results.result: Neuronal hUCP2 increases health and longevity while increasing glycolysis and decreasing ROS, moderate pan-neuronal hUCP3 modestly extends male lifespan, but stronger hUCP3 expression in neurons or mNSC decreases lifespan possibly by increasing DILP levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C159 are supported by citations to Fridell et al., 2005 and Humphrey et al., 2009, demonstrating dose-dependent and sex-specific effects of uncoupling proteins.

results.result: Fly muscles accumulate protein aggregates with age, and maintenance of proteostasis is enhanced in long-lived animals through FOXO target genes like 4E-BP, with muscle FOXO signaling through 4E-BP decreasing feeding and insulin release to delay aggregate accumulation in other tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C162 are supported by citation to Demontis and Perrimon, 2010 and established knowledge, demonstrating muscle-to-brain signaling affecting proteostasis.

results.result: Overexpression of hedgehog extends lifespan while disruption shortens it and decreases dopaminergic neurons, with glial but not neuronal overexpression sufficient for lifespan extension, and glial hsp69/hsp40 overexpression rescuing hh mutant lifespan and partially rescuing Aβ42 toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C167 are all supported by citation to Rallis et al., 2020, identifying a novel role for glial hedgehog signaling in longevity.

results.result: Exposure to live yeast odor partially reverses DR-mediated longevity, and loss of Orco function significantly increases fly lifespan independent of food intake, activity, respiration, or reproduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C170 are supported by citation to Libert et al., 2007, establishing food perception as a modulator of DR effects in flies.

results.result: Mutation of the water sensor ppk28 extends Drosophila lifespan by up to 40% requiring AKH receptor, with higher AKH protein levels in mutants and activation of Akh-expressing neurons sufficient to recapitulate the lifespan effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C171 and C172 are supported by citation to Waterson et al., 2014, demonstrating water sensing effects on longevity.

results.result: Gustatory perception is necessary for normal stress resistance and lifespan in low-glucose environments, loss of sweet taste receptor Gr64 produces sleep impairment and extends lifespan despite increased eating, loss of trehalose receptor Gr5a decreases lifespan without altering feeding, and loss of labellar taste bristles requires insulin signaling to extend lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C177 are supported by citations to Linford et al., 2015; Ostojic et al., 2014; and Waterson et al., 2015, demonstrating bidirectional effects of taste perception on longevity.

results.result: The effects of dietary restriction on aging in Drosophila are predominantly influenced by dietary composition (mainly protein content) rather than overall caloric content.
results.evaluation: Claim C178 is supported by citations to Solon-Biet et al., 2014; Mair et al., 2005; Skorupa et al., 2008; and Simpson and Raubenheimer, 2007, establishing the importance of macronutrient composition.

results.result: Flies exposed to essential amino acid restriction behaviorally switch from sugar to protein preference, requiring both serotonin signaling through 5-HT2A receptor and dopaminergic circuit plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C179 and C180 are supported by citations to Steck et al., 2018; Ro et al., 2016; and Liu et al., 2017, demonstrating neural control of feeding behavior.

results.result: When sugar and protein are presented separately allowing behavioral diet construction, flies live shorter than with a complete diet, requiring serotonin signaling through 5-HT2A, with serotonin, 5-HT2A, and the amino acid transporter JhI-21 modulating diet-dependent aging by ascribing value to protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C183 are supported by citations to Ro et al., 2016 and related studies, with C183 being a reasonable inference about inter-tissue communication based on JhI-21 expression in reproductive tissues.

results.result: Exposure to female sex pheromones without mating causes rapid reversible declines in fat stores, stress resistance, and longevity in male flies through taste perception via ppk23 and neuronal signaling involving NPF/NPY and FOXO, with effects partially reversed by copulation through circuits perceiving reproductive reward.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C187 are supported by citations to Gendron et al., 2014 and Harvanek et al., 2017, demonstrating neural control of reproduction-longevity tradeoffs.

results.result: Drosophila can visually perceive dead conspecifics inducing short- and long-term effects on health and longevity, with exposure decreasing starvation resistance, depleting lipid storage, and shortening lifespan through serotonin signaling via 5-HT2A receptor.
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C190 are supported by citation to Chakraborty et al., 2019, demonstrating visual perception effects on longevity.

results.result: Gr63a encodes part of a CO2 receptor that detects alarm cues at low concentrations, and loss-of-function mutation in Gr63a extends lifespan additively with ab1C neuronal ablation, suggesting DR and alarm-sensing act through distinct pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C191 and C192 are supported by citations to Suh et al., 2007 and Poon et al., 2010, demonstrating alarm cue perception effects on longevity.

results.result: Reduced insulin and growth hormone signaling significantly increase mouse lifespan, with Ames and Snell dwarf mice living 40% longer with decreased plasma IGF-1, becoming obese in old age, and not rescued by adult pituitary grafting, with the mechanism likely involving IGF-1 based on similar results from GHR-KO, IGF-I receptor heterozygous null, and Ghrhr knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C198 are supported by citations to Brown-Borg et al., 1996; Flurkey et al., 2002; Flurkey et al., 2001; Coschigano et al., 2003; Holzenberger et al., 2003, establishing conservation of insulin/IGF signaling effects in mammals.

results.result: Partial loss of function of IGF-1R in neurons during development leads to reduced growth and lifespan extension, with these mice gaining more weight with age and having higher adipose tissue, leptin, and lipids, demonstrating that decreased insulin signaling can alter global metabolism and extend lifespan in mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C199-C201 are supported by citation to Kappeler et al., 2008, demonstrating neuronal control of mammalian longevity through insulin signaling.

results.result: In humans, insulin regulation, sensitivity, and neuronal excitability positively correlate with longevity, with the transcriptional repressor REST negatively regulating neural excitation and FOXO1 expression and positively correlating with longevity, and C. elegans REST orthologues required for daf-2 knockout lifespan extension.
results.evaluation: Claims C202-C204 are supported by citation to Zullo et al., 2019, providing evidence for conservation of neuronal excitability effects on longevity in humans.

results.result: The locus encoding tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), insulin (INS), and IGF2 correlates with longevity in centenarians, with TH being the rate-limiting enzyme for dopamine production, and polymorphisms in TH-INS associated with female lifespan and TH-IGF2 with male lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C205-C208 are supported by citations to De Luca et al., 2001 and Nagatsu, 1995, providing human genetic evidence for neuronal signaling effects on longevity.

results.result: A cohort of 90-109 year-olds had 66% higher incidence of the DRD4 7R allele correlating with higher physical activity, and DRD4 knockout in mice leads to ~8% decrease in lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C209 and C210 are supported by citation to Grady et al., 2013, providing additional human genetic evidence linking dopamine signaling to longevity.

results.result: Mice heterozygous at the Irs2 locus have increased insulin sensitivity and live ~25% longer, with neuronal Irs2 knockout sufficient to phenocopy this and leading to decreased Sod2 and Foxo1 mRNA expression, supporting that reduced neuronal insulin signaling modulates lifespan through enhanced oxidative stress protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C211-C214 are supported by citation to Taguchi et al., 2007, demonstrating neuronal insulin signaling effects on mammalian longevity.

results.result: Intranasal administration of recombinant human Hsp70 to middle-aged and elderly mice extends lifespan by ~10% and improves learning and memory, with treated mice having higher neuronal density in temporal cortex and hippocampus and more proteasomal subunit accumulation, suggesting Hsp70 promotes proteasomal activity through cell autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C215-C218 are supported by citation to Bobkova et al., 2015, demonstrating a potential therapeutic intervention targeting proteostasis.

results.result: The hypothalamus is a key producer of neuropeptides and hormones and is key to maintaining homeostasis in energy balance, blood pressure, oxygenation, body temperature, and circadian rhythm.
results.evaluation: Claims C219 and C220 are supported by citation to Barbosa et al., 2017 and established knowledge, providing context for subsequent hypothalamic studies.

results.result: Overexpressing UCP2 in mouse hypocretin neurons increases hypothalamic temperature and decreases core body temperature by 0.3-0.5°C, with transgenic mice having the same calorie intake but living 12-20% longer, suggesting neuronal regulation of body temperature influences lifespan independently of dietary restriction.
results.evaluation: Claims C221-C223 are supported by citation to Conti et al., 2006, demonstrating hypothalamic control of longevity through temperature regulation.

results.result: NF-κB is involved with inflammation and immune response, and middle-aged mice with activated hypothalamic NF-κB have shorter lifespan while inhibition extends lifespan by ~15% and improves multiple healthspan measures, with hypothalamic microglial NF-κB knockout sufficient to phenocopy the effect and both neuronal and glial knockdown increasing GnRH mRNA expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C224-C229 are supported by citations to Taniguchi and Karin, 2018 and Zhang et al., 2013, demonstrating hypothalamic inflammation effects on longevity.

results.result: GnRH neurons regulate fertility through pulsatile GnRH release, and increases in GnRH expression or treatment correlate with improved neurogenesis and lifespan, with the implication that increased inflammation from NF-κB during aging leads to loss of GnRH release and diminished health that can be reversed by restoring GnRH levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C230-C233 are supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013 and established knowledge, with C232-C233 being reasonable inferences from the data.

results.result: Brain-specific Sirt1 overexpression (BRASTO) mice live 10-15% longer with decreased cancer incidence and improved healthspan parameters including increased physical activity, higher core body temperature, more oxygen consumption, and more non-REM sleep, with similar traits correlated with increased quality of life in elderly humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C234-C236 are supported by citations to Satoh et al., 2013; Rea et al., 2015; Spadafora et al., 1996; and Simonsick et al., 2016, demonstrating brain Sirt1 effects on longevity and healthspan.

results.result: BRASTO mice show increased skeletal muscle mitochondria and mitochondrial functional gene expression as well as higher mRNA expression of markers of neuronal activity in hypothalamic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C237 and C238 are supported by citation to Satoh et al., 2013, though the causative mechanisms remain incompletely characterized.

results.result: Cellular senescence is characterized by permanent cessation of cellular proliferation, and there is evidence that proliferation of senescent cells throughout an animal's lifetime accelerates aging via pro-inflammatory secreted compounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C239 and C240 are supported by established knowledge in the field, providing context for subsequent senescence studies.

results.result: PAI-1, a neuronally expressed protein, regulates cellular senescence in mammals, and klotho knockout mice exhibit accelerated aging with increased plasma PAI-1, with PAI-1 knockout in klotho mutants reducing senescence and completely rescuing lifespan, likely due to accumulation of pro-inflammatory molecules from the senescence messaging secretome, with elevated PAI-1 levels in humans associated with aging disease states.
results.evaluation: Claims C241-C245 are supported by citations to Carmeliet et al., 1993; Eren et al., 2002; Eren et al., 2014; and Yamamoto et al., 2005, demonstrating a role for neuronal PAI-1 in senescence and aging.

results.result: Mammals accumulate senescent cells throughout life, and when chronically present they exacerbate age-dependent tissue deterioration through SASP, but when transiently present they can promote healthy outcomes like optimal wound healing.
results.evaluation: Claims C246-C248 are supported by citations to Campisi and Robert, 2014 and Demaria et al., 2014, highlighting the context-dependent effects of senescent cells.

results.result: Many anti-aging therapeutics that extend mouse lifespan target and kill senescent cells, and senolytic compounds have entered clinical trials to test efficacy in treating age-associated diseases.
results.evaluation: Claims C249 and C250 are supported by citations to Campisi et al., 2019 and Kulkarni et al., 2020, highlighting the therapeutic potential of targeting senescent cells.

results.result: Circulating factors in young mouse blood can restore cellular function in older mice, with old mice exposed to young serum showing enhanced Notch signaling in satellite cells, increased hepatocyte proliferation, enhanced neurogenesis, decreased cardiac hypertrophy, and reduced SASP response.
results.evaluation: Claims C251 and C252 are supported by citations to Conboy et al., 2005; Loffredo et al., 2013; Katsimpardi et al., 2014; Rebo et al., 2016; and Yousefzadeh et al., 2020, demonstrating systemic effects of circulating factors.

results.result: The TGF-β superfamily member GDF11 decreases with age and restoring its levels is sufficient to reverse age-related dysfunction in the skeletal system and restore the neurogenic niche.
results.evaluation: Claims C253 and C254 are supported by citations to Sinha et al., 2014 and Katsimpardi et al., 2014, identifying GDF11 as a key circulating factor.

results.result: An initial study found that young plasma is not able to extend lifespan in aged mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C255 is supported by citation to Shytikov et al., 2014, providing an important caveat to the parabiosis findings.

results.result: Global TRPV1 knockout in mice increases metabolic activity and lifespan by 10-20% without changing body weight or GH/IGF-1, requiring CRTC-1 in worms, with TRPV-1 necessary for CRTC-1 nuclear translocation in mouse DRG neurons where CRTC-1 interacts with CREB to regulate neuropeptide secretion at pancreatic beta cells, leading to reduced CGRP expression and increased insulin secretion for better glucose tolerance and longevity.
results.evaluation: Claims C256-C260 are supported by citation to Riera et al., 2014, demonstrating conservation of TRPV signaling effects from worms to mammals.

results.result: Recent data from invertebrates supports non-canonical cell non-autonomous mechanisms where peripheral tissues use retrograde signals back to the nervous system to maintain or modify physiology.
results.evaluation: Claim C261 is supported by citations to Minniti et al., 2019; Bouagnon et al., 2019; Demontis and Perrimon, 2010; and Ulgherait et al., 2014, introducing the concept of retrograde signaling.

results.result: Just a day of hypoxia can extend lifespan in a worm, though whether this is due to persistent physiological changes or lasting epigenetic changes remains an open question.
results.evaluation: Claim C262 is supported by citation to Mehta et al., 2009, raising important questions about the temporal dynamics of longevity interventions.

results.result: Serotonin antagonism can extend adult neuroplasticity and lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claim C263 is supported by citations to Petrascheck et al., 2009 and Bazopoulou et al., 2017, suggesting therapeutic potential of serotonin modulation.

results.result: Two drug combinations synergistically improve lifespan and healthspan in C. elegans, requiring TGF-β signaling and increased levels of monounsaturated fatty acids.
results.evaluation: Claim C264 is supported by citation to Admasu et al., 2018, demonstrating the potential for combinatorial therapeutic approaches.

results.result: Simultaneous inhibition of MEK, mTORC1, and GSK-3 acted additively to increase Drosophila lifespan by 48%.
results.evaluation: Claim C265 is supported by citation to Castillo-Quan et al., 2019, demonstrating additive effects of targeting multiple pathways in flies.
